About

I'm a Mechanical Engineering student, Class of 2028, at Cornell's College of Engineering, minoring in Spanish. I've found that I do my best work when I'm challenged — whether that's an engineering team, a class, or a project I've taken on myself. I thrive on pushing my limits and tackling problems with grit, creativity, and stubborn persistence until the answer takes shape, and I care about understanding a project deeply enough to bring real technical thinking to it, not just a finished part.

Most of my project work lives in two places: Cornell University Unmanned Air Systems (CUAir), where I test and validate a competition aircraft's structure and instrumentation, and a summer spent inside a ski manufacturing shop learning how a product actually gets made, not just designed. Alongside that, I've worked on smaller team builds, including a mechanical filtration prototype for agricultural pest mitigation.

01 / 06

Wing Loading Test Rig

Integration & Testing, CUAir — Cornell University Unmanned Air Systems
ROLE
Test Lead, Wing Loading
TOOLS
XFLR5, Desmos, hand analysis
TARGET
Factor of safety, 3G loading
OUTPUT
Reconfigurable whiffletree rig
Full CAD assembly of the wing loading test rig (WLTR), showing the whiffletree mechanism that distributes load across both wings

Background

CUAir's competition aircraft is carbon-fiber and student-built, which means its wings need to be validated against real flight loading before every competition season — not just trusted on paper. The prior semester's process used AVL to gather lift data on the aircraft, then hand calculations to place a handful of clamps, with sandbags and buckets of weight used to simulate loading while the team listened for cracking noises and watched for visible failure or wingtip deflection. It worked, but the load distribution across the wing was approximate, and the setup wasn't something we could confidently rebuild the next time a wing needed testing. My goal this cycle was to make the rig both more accurate and repeatable — ensuring the wing's stability under loading that actually resembles flight conditions.

Requirements

I defined the rig around three functional requirements: it had to allow qualitative evaluation of plane systems through direct observation (cracking, visible failure), provide quantitative analysis by measuring wingtip deflection, and be recreatable so future teams could re-test a wing without starting from scratch. On the non-functional side, testing had to use the existing WLTR setup on campus, and needed to support additional testing across variable airspeed, angle of attack, and bank angle — not just a single static load case.

Deriving the Load Distribution

Rather than estimating clamp placement by hand, I used XFLR5 to run a more advanced lift analysis with angle of attack, bank angle, and velocity as variables, letting me find the wing's maximum expected lift after optimizing for these parameters rather than assuming a single flight condition. That gave me an accurate lift curve to work from instead of a rough approximation.

From the XFLR5 output, I built a lift function as a function of position along the wing, then modeled it in Desmos as a piecewise function that assumed the fuselage itself generates no lift. I integrated that function across eight spanwise sections to approximate the point forces acting at each section, then summed those to find the total lift on one side of the wing. Each section's fraction of that total gave me the exact percentage of total lift that needed to be applied at each clamp point.

Working through the piecewise lift function and spanwise integration in Desmos
Section (tip → fuselage)% of total wing lift
Section 1 (tip)14.24%
Section 224.49%
Section 329.41%
Section 4 (fuselage)31.86%

Solving the Whiffletree

With the lift percentages known, I used predetermined span distances — a full span of 2.52 m, a fuselage span of 0.18 m, and a resulting span of 1.17 m per side — to set up moment balance equations and solve for equilibrium at each clamp position. I then worked the whiffletree itself: a hanging-beam mechanism where each successive beam splits the load in the correct ratio between two connection points below it. Solving that system meant working upward through nested ratios of lift and beam width, using the predetermined clamp spacing to find each connection point, and labeling the diagram as I solved so the geometry stayed traceable.

Designing the Clamps

The whiffletree math only mattered if each clamp actually delivered its calculated share of the load to the right point on the wing without damaging the wing's surface. I built each clamp around a padded wood block — layering dense foam over the contact face and wrapping it in cloth tape — so the clamping force spread across a wide, cushioned area instead of concentrating at a hard edge or corner. Each clamp carries a steel eye-hook to connect up to its point on the whiffletree above, and every clamp had to be positioned at the exact spanwise location the moment-balance calculations called for, so the load applied through it matched the percentage of total lift assigned to that section.

Result & Next Steps

The finished rig let us test to a factor of safety of 3G under a realistic, non-uniform load distribution instead of an evenly-spaced approximation, while still recording the same qualitative (audible/visible failure) and quantitative (deflection) data the requirements called for. Heading into the next design cycle, I identified follow-up work: reconfiguring the WLTR for Hermes, a smaller aircraft that would let us shrink the rig's footprint; researching load cells to replace sandbags with more controlled, incremental loading; and using XFLR5 to test additional bank-angle cases that would reveal how the wing holds up under more concentrated, uneven loads.

02 / 06

Camera Tracker Gimbal Tuning

Integration & Testing, CUAir — Cornell University Unmanned Air Systems
ROLE
Design & Integration
HARDWARE
Sony A7III, 3-axis gimbal
CORE ISSUE
Wiring tangle + servo jitter
OUTPUT
Slip-ring redesign, damping fix
CAD assembly of the camera tracker gimbal, sized to carry a full Sony A7III body and lens

Background

CUAir needs smooth, consistent footage of its competition aircraft for judging, including tight overhead passes where the plane crosses almost directly above the camera. The team's existing options — an antenna tracker or a simpler gimbal — couldn't do the job: too few axes to hold a stable orientation through a continuous pass, and neither could physically mount a full camera body with a lens attached. The previous year, a teammate had designed and built a 2.5-axis gimbal to solve this, and my work picked up from there — tuning two problems that showed up once the gimbal was in real use: wiring that could tangle itself during continuous rotation, and servo motion that was too abrupt for smooth video.

Requirements

The gimbal had to track the plane smoothly at all times with the Sony A7III mounted, without the wiring ever restricting motion or getting stressed by it, while resisting 20 mph wind gusts and standing up to extended outdoor use without overheating or deforming. On the usability side, it needed to assemble in under 15 minutes by one person, pack into an SKB case, keep every critical part to an ultimate safety factor of 2, and still leave room for camera CG adjustment and an onboard display screen.

Problem 1 — Wiring Integration

The gimbal's continuous-rotation servos meant that after enough rotation in one direction, wires would start pulling and tangling — with the yaw axis being the most likely to fail, since it was the axis most likely to see a full 360° rotation and had to carry its own wiring plus both other motors'. I compared three approaches to solve it:

REJECTED

Wire slack + spool

Extending wires with a take-up spool would limit total rotations before needing a manual reset — not workable for continuous tracking.

REJECTED

Limit axis rotation

Capping rotation to under 360° would defeat the purpose of using continuous-rotation servos and hurt yaw tracking specifically.

CHOSEN

Slip rings

Transfers power and signal between stationary and rotating wiring with unlimited 360° rotation — integrated into each axis that needed it.

Slip rings solved the rotation problem, but fitting one required its own design work: it had to sit centered on the servo's axis of rotation, mount to a stationary base, and use a hollow bore with a drive shaft to spin with the motor. I first tried fitting a small slip ring between the motor's stator and rotor directly, but the motor couldn't be safely disassembled, and I didn't trust a modified motor to hold up reliably. I redesigned around a stacked configuration instead — slip ring mounted above the servo, connected through its own drive shaft — which added a mounting bracket and a slightly taller assembly, but kept the motor untouched and the slip ring properly centered.

Problem 2 — Servo Control

Separately, the servo motors themselves moved too abruptly for smooth footage — overhead passes in particular need high-precision, rapid adjustments without any jerkiness showing up on camera. I evaluated three fixes:

REJECTED

Servo horn linkage

Pairing a longer servo arm with a shorter output arm trades speed for torque, but sacrifices total range of motion — unusable on yaw.

REJECTED

Gear reduction

Adjustable via gear ratio, but introduces backlash — play in the gears when reversing direction that would throw off tracking precision.

CHOSEN — near term

Damping grease

Smooths servo response directly with minimal added parts or space — best fit for the system with the least disruption elsewhere.

OptionViscosityNotes
Nye Nyogel 767A28,185 cStIndustry-standard "one size fits all"; reapply every 2–5 yrs
eXcelerate Damper Grease100k–200k cStPrecise viscosity increments; check every 1–3 months
Tribosyn 320 SeriesUp to 28k cStSilicone-free (safer near electronics); lasts 5+ yrs — selected

Takeaways

The slip-ring redesign resolved the wiring tangle without sacrificing continuous rotation, and Tribosyn damping grease gave the servos noticeably smoother motion without adding mechanical complexity. Looking ahead, I flagged that a positional encoder is likely still necessary on the servos for tracking precision the damping alone can't fully deliver.

Production Optimization — Base Cutting

Mechanical Engineering Intern, Meier Skis — Denver, CO
MATERIAL
Dura Surf 4000 sintered base
TOOL
Dragknife, Shop Sabre CNC
METHOD
Iterative toolpath design
RESULT
57% faster base production

Background

Every ski starts with a base — in this case, Dura Surf 4000, a sintered polyethylene material that has to be cut to the exact profile of the ski before it's laminated into the rest of the construction. The cutting method used for this step directly sets the pace for how many bases the shop can produce, so it was a natural place to look for a production bottleneck.

Approach

I developed a new production method for cutting Dura Surf 4000 base material using a dragknife on the shop's Shop Sabre CNC — a tool that drags an angled blade through the material rather than routing or lasering it. Because a dragknife cuts differently than a rotating tool, the toolpath itself needed to be designed and iterated on specifically for this blade geometry, rather than reused from an existing router program. I worked through several toolpath variations to make sure the cut consistently held the tolerance requirements the base shape demanded, then tested each variation directly on the CNC to check both cut quality and cycle time.

A pair of finished bases straight off the dragknife-cut toolpath — clean edges, held to the tolerance the base shape required

Result

The final toolpath and cutting method reduced base production time by 57% compared to the prior process, while still holding the tolerances the base geometry required — a meaningful throughput gain on a step that every ski has to go through.

Custom Display Mount Fabrication

Mechanical Engineering Intern, Meier Skis — Denver, CO
SOFTWARE
Fusion 360
PROCESS
CNC machining + hand finishing
OUTPUT
14 mounts + 1 tap handle
ADJACENT WORK
5 ski graphics, Photoshop

Background

Meier displays a rotating lineup of skis in-shop and at events, and each ski needs a mount that holds it securely and shows it off well — a generic mount doesn't work across the lineup, since every ski model has a different width and top-sheet profile.

Design & Fabrication

I designed 14 custom-engraved display mounts in Fusion 360, altering each one's geometry to match the specific width and top profile of the ski it was built for rather than using one universal design. Each mount was CNC-machined, then hand-finished and post-processed so the final piece looked as polished as the skis it was displaying — this was hardware meant to be seen, not just functional. Alongside the mounts, I designed and fabricated a personalized tap handle using the same Fusion 360 and CNC workflow.

A finished mount — hand-stained wood with a CNC-engraved logo inlay, hand-painted and post-processed for display

Graphics Collaboration

Separately from the mount work, I created 5 custom ski graphics in Adobe Photoshop, working with the design team to make sure each one met production graphic standards before going to print — a chance to bridge the mechanical and visual sides of the product.

05 / 06

Vibrating Filtration System for Spotted Lanternfly Mitigation

Team Project — Vineyard Harvesting Application
PROBLEM
SLF contamination in grape harvest
APPROACH
Mechanical separation, not chemical
STATIC LOAD
Tested to 100 lbs
OUTPUT
Working prototype, field-ready design
The finished prototype: perforated tray, adjustable aluminum frame, and cable suspension system

The Problem

Spotted Lanternflies (SLF) contaminate grapes during harvesting by releasing chemicals that taint the juice and reduce fruit quality, often making the affected grapes unsuitable for processing entirely. Since grapes are sold by weight, every ounce of usable product matters directly to revenue — and SLF infestations have already caused significant economic damage across the Northeast, with losses climbing as the infestation spreads and marketable yield drops. The core sub-problem is straightforward but costly: SLF end up mixed into the grape harvest during collection, and the longer they sit in that mixture, the worse the contamination gets.

The target environment: a mechanical harvester and field gondola, where the device would sit during collection

Design Goal

We focused the design on saving as much of the usable grape harvest as possible, even at the cost of losing a small percentage of solids. Straining the liquid out lets harvesters keep the more valuable product, while separating out the solids makes SLF contamination easy to spot and remove. We prioritized a simple, mechanical approach — reliable, easy to use, and adjustable enough to retrofit onto the harvester gondolas vineyards already use, rather than requiring new equipment entirely.

The Prototype

The final device is a vibrating filtration system built to sit inside a vineyard gondola during harvesting, letting juice pass through while retaining solids. It has four main components: a perforated PVC tray that allows juice through while catching solids and SLF material, an adjustable aluminum frame with a pin-lock mechanism for height adjustment, a cable suspension system that provides tension support and reduces structural stress on the frame, and a motor-driven vibration linkage that generates controlled vibration to prevent clogging and keep flow moving.

Testing Methods

  • Draining flow rate — tested under two pour conditions to see how input height and flow distribution affect drainage: a direct vertical pour straight onto the flat surface measured 3.26 oz/sec/sq in, while a second test poured from several inches above to spread flow across the surface.
  • Static load capacity — the tray and frame were loaded to a maximum tested weight of 100 lbs without failure.
  • Dynamic load — we simulated falling grapes by dropping 40 bolts (14.3 g each) from a height of 1 m onto the straining surface, using the impact as an estimate for loading from actual grapes (roughly 5 g each).
  • Oscillation — the vibration linkage was tuned to an amplitude of 2 cm at a frequency of 1.11 Hz.
Dynamic load test — weighted bolts dropped onto the straining surface to simulate falling grapes

Conclusion & Future Work

The final prototype successfully reduced contamination through mechanical separation while preserving usable grape juice during harvest, and testing showed the system was structurally sound, stable, and effective at filtering juice while retaining solids. The clearest next steps: adding adjustable motor speed control to vary vibration frequency and optimize performance, running chemical validation on collected juice to confirm contamination reduction, and conducting long-term field testing across multiple vineyards and conditions to evaluate durability.

06 / 06

Torsion Testing

Integration & Testing, CUAir — Cornell University Unmanned Air Systems
STATUS
Research & planning
LOAD CASE
Boom-induced torsion on the mid-wing
PLATFORM
WLTR, small-increment mass loading
NEXT MILESTONE
Design review this semester
Project status: I originated this test and am currently developing the research and project proposal, which I will present at CUAir's design review this semester. The method below is a tentative plan, not a finished result.

Background

Our wing loading tests validate the structure against lift, but the mid-wing carries another load that none of our current testing examines: torsion. The booms attach to the wing at a distance from its spanwise axis, so whenever a boom pitches up or down instead of staying horizontal, its connection to the wing generates a moment about the spanwise axis and twists the mid-wing. Torsion Testing is a proposed ground test that applies representative torsional loads to the mid-wing, so we can see how it holds up to this load case on the ground before it has to in flight.

Understanding where that torque comes from has been part of the work. Through conversations with teammates on the flight and electrical side, my current understanding is that on Hermes the dominant source is differential thrust: when the aircraft yaws, motors at opposite ends of the booms spin at different speeds, and that thrust imbalance twists the booms against the wing. I'm working with them to pull motor RPM logs from past flights, including the largest RPM differentials, as a first estimate of the torsional load, along with the maximum RPM expected in normal flight to define a worst case.

Research Findings

I surveyed torsion testing practices in aviation and other industries and reached a clear conclusion: most established methods depend on loading and measurement equipment that is far beyond a student team's budget. Rather than adapting an industry rig, I developed a tentative, low-cost method built around infrastructure we already have and trust.

Proposed Test Method

  • Familiar setup — configure the WLTR to closely resemble the wing loading test, using the exact same mount to the mid-wing so the boundary conditions match a setup we already understand.
  • Test article — the mid-wing and booms, and possibly the wingtips, depending on whether they turn out to be affected by torsion (still to be determined).
  • New whiffletree — a beam oriented in the direction of the booms, with rings on the bar so a cable can connect to the ends of each boom through custom boom linkages. Whether the cable should pull straight up is still an open design question.
  • Incremental loading — add mass as in wing loading, but in much smaller increments, until the target loading condition is reached.
  • Measurement — torsional strain throughout the mid-wing, with strain gauges as the leading candidate.

Defining the Loading Condition

The target can be set either as a torque load or as a torsion deflection angle. For an otherwise unchanging beam the two are proportional to each other, so whichever is easier to extract from Hermes data can drive the test. Recording both would go a step further: with torque and twist angle known, I could solve backward for the mid-wing's shear modulus and polar moment of inertia properties, turning the test into a way to characterize the structure as well as validate it.

Finding the Shear Center

My research also showed that locating the shear center of the wings would be ideal, and may be necessary if the loading conditions are based on torque. Calculating it analytically would be very difficult given the internal structure of Hermes, so the plan is to find it experimentally, most likely with strain gauges.

Next Steps

  • Turn the flight-log RPM data and propeller thrust coefficients into a meaningful estimate of the torsional load on the mid-wing.
  • Decide the loading metric (torque versus deflection angle) and the direction of cable pull.
  • Determine whether the wingtips need to be included in the test article.
  • Plan the strain gauge layout for both strain measurement and the shear center search.
  • Present the proposal at design review this semester.
